title: Jump Game II
description: Find the minimum number of jumps to reach the end using an implicit BFS with a greedy reach pointer.

data.text: You are given a 0-indexed array `nums` where `nums[i]` is the maximum jump length from index `i`. You start at index 0 and the array is guaranteed reachable. Return the minimum number of jumps to reach the last index.

**Input:** `nums = [2, 3, 1, 1, 4]`

**Output:** `2`

**Explanation:** Jump from index 0 to 1 (covering 2 units), then 3 units to the last index.

Think of it as BFS over positions, where each jump count is a layer. From every index reachable in `j` jumps, note how far you can get in `j + 1` jumps — the maximum of `i + nums[i]`. When your current position passes the end of the current layer, you have used one more jump. You never need a queue because the layers are contiguous ranges.

data.title: Greedy BFS — O(n) time
data.content: Track the end of the current jump layer and the farthest reach the next layer can achieve.

data.title: Greedy choice is safe: take the farthest reach
data.text: Within one layer, all positions cost the same number of jumps. So the only thing that matters is which position reaches furthest — you should always extend to `max(i + nums[i])`. There is no benefit to a shorter jump.

data.title: Loop to n - 1, not n
data.text: Stop the loop at `n - 2`. Once you can reach the last index, no further jump is needed; iterating one step too far can add a spurious extra jump.

The DP formulation — `dp[i]` is the minimum jumps to reach `i` — is O(n²) and correct, but the greedy version is strictly better because the cost function is uniform. Recognise the BFS shape and drop the table.

data.title: DP for reference — O(n²)
data.content: Useful for checking the greedy result on small inputs.

data.caption: Each layer is the set of indices reachable with the same number of jumps; the greedy reach extends only the next layer.

cards.title: Greedy BFS layers
cards.description: Track current layer end and next reach

data.title: Complete solution
data.content: The uniform-cost structure is what makes greed valid: this problem is BFS in disguise, and BFS processes nodes in layers. The 'Jump Game I' existence question has an even simpler greedy rule — just track whether you ever fall behind `i`.
